## Half Lit, Always

Here is the fact that fixes almost every misunderstanding about the Moon: **the Moon is always half lit.** Right now, whatever shape you see in the sky, exactly half of the Moon is in sunlight and half is in darkness. It has to be. The Moon is a ball, and a ball near a lamp is always lit on the side facing the lamp.

So why does it look like a thin sliver one week and a full circle two weeks later?

Because the Moon **orbits** Earth, and as it moves, we see the lit half from different angles. When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, its lit half faces away from us and we see almost nothing. That is a **new moon**. A week later the Moon has moved a quarter of the way around, and we see half of the lit half — a **first quarter** moon, which looks like a half circle. Another week and the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun. Now its whole lit half faces us: a **full moon**. Another week: **third quarter**, the other half circle. In between those four, the Moon is a thin **crescent** or a fat **gibbous**. While the lit part grows toward full we call it **waxing**; while it shrinks toward new, **waning**. The whole cycle of **phases** takes about 29.5 days.

Notice what did not appear in that explanation: Earth's shadow. The phases are not shadows at all. They are just the angle from which we look at a half-lit ball. You can prove it tonight with a lamp and a ball: hold the ball at arm's length, turn slowly, and watch the phases roll across it. Earth's shadow plays no part in it.

So when does Earth's shadow matter? During a **lunar eclipse**, when the full Moon passes through Earth's shadow and turns a dim copper red for an hour or two. That happens only a few times a year, not every month, because the Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees. Most months the full Moon passes a little above or below the shadow and misses it.

A **solar eclipse** is the reverse: the new Moon passes exactly between Earth and the Sun and casts its own small shadow onto Earth. Only people standing inside that shadow, a path a few hundred kilometers wide, see the Sun blocked. The Moon is about 400 times smaller than the Sun, but it is also about 400 times closer, which is the coincidence that lets it cover the Sun so neatly.

One more thing you have probably noticed without noticing. The Moon always shows us the same face. It **rotates** once for every orbit, so the same side stays pointed at Earth. Nobody saw the far side until a spacecraft photographed it in 1959.

Half lit, always. Hold onto that sentence and the rest of the sky falls into place.

## Moonlight and Changing Views

Outside a lunar eclipse, approximately half of the Moon receives sunlight. The Moon is a sphere: its Sun-facing hemisphere is illuminated, while its other hemisphere has night. A phase describes how much of the illuminated hemisphere we see from Earth, not how much of the entire Moon receives sunlight.

As the Moon orbits Earth, our viewing angle changes. At new moon, the Moon is in the Sun's direction and its illuminated hemisphere faces mostly away from us. At first quarter, roughly a week later, half of the visible disk is illuminated. At full moon, the Moon is opposite the Sun in our sky and we see its illuminated face. Third quarter shows the other half disk. A crescent has less than half of its visible disk illuminated; a gibbous has more than half but less than all. Waxing means that visible illuminated fraction is growing toward full; waning means it is shrinking toward new.

The phase cycle averages 29.5 days. The Moon orbits Earth and rotates once in about 27.3 days relative to distant stars. The phase cycle is longer because Earth and the Moon also travel around the Sun: the Moon must move farther to reach the same Sun-Earth-Moon angle again.

Ordinary phases are not caused by Earth's cast shadow. The boundary between the Moon's own day and night is called the terminator. Model phases with a cool LED lamp and a ball on a blunt handle, under teacher supervision. Hold the ball at arm's length and turn to change the viewing angle. Near full moon, hold it slightly above your head's shadow so your body does not cause an accidental eclipse. Keep the ball out of that shadow unless you deliberately demonstrate an eclipse. Never use direct solar viewing or a laser for this activity.

A lunar eclipse happens at full moon when the Moon enters Earth's shadow. It can be penumbral, partial or total. During totality the Moon often looks copper red because sunlight filtered and bent through Earth's atmosphere reaches it. A lunar eclipse can be observed where the Moon is above the horizon and weather permits.

A solar eclipse happens at new moon when the Moon blocks some or all of the Sun for observers in the affected part of Earth. A total eclipse has a narrow path of totality, with a wider region seeing a partial eclipse. An annular eclipse leaves a bright ring because the Moon appears too small to cover the Sun completely. Never look directly at the Sun during this classroom investigation.

Eclipses do not happen every month. The Moon's orbital plane is tilted about five degrees to Earth's orbital plane around the Sun. Most new and full moons miss the necessary alignment; eclipses require alignment near where those planes cross. Our flat diagrams omit that tilt and are not to scale.

The Moon rotates once per orbit, so approximately the same face stays toward Earth. Small apparent rocking motions, called libration, let us see a little around its edges over time. The far side is not permanently dark. Phase pictures can appear rotated with viewing location and time; our right-lit waxing examples use a northern-up textbook convention.

from: Because the Moon is up for about twelve hours out of every twenty-four, and half of that time is daylight. It is easiest to spot near first and third quarter, when it is high in the sky while the Sun is still up.
to: The Moon can be above the horizon during daylight and bright enough to see against the sky. Visibility depends on phase, location, time and conditions. First-quarter Moon is often visible in the afternoon, and third-quarter Moon in the morning.

from: There is a far side we never see from Earth, but it is not always dark. It gets just as much sunlight as the near side; it is simply pointed away from us. 'Dark side' is a great album title and a bad astronomy term.
to: The far side mostly faces away from Earth, but it receives sunlight too. The Moon’s own night moves around it. Libration lets us see a little around the edges over time; far side does not mean permanently dark.

from: Orange comes from looking through more air, which scatters away blue light, the same reason sunsets are orange. Huge is an illusion: measure it with your thumb at the horizon and again overhead and it is the same size.
to: Near the horizon, moonlight passes through more air, which scatters away more blue light and can leave an orange appearance. The striking increase in apparent size is mainly a perceptual illusion. Its angular size changes little during that short rise, though Earth-Moon distance changes its actual angular size over an orbit.

from: Same phase on the same night, but flipped. Someone in Australia sees the crescent lit on the opposite side from someone in Canada, because they are looking at the Moon while standing upside down relative to each other.
to: Observers see essentially the same phase at the same time, but it can appear rotated with location and time. Northern and southern views often have opposite orientations. Right-lit does not universally mean waxing; follow the illuminated fraction across successive days.

from: Because the Moon's shadow is small and Earth is big, so any one spot sees totality only about once every few hundred years. People travel across the world for those few minutes of daytime darkness.
to: Totality crosses a narrow path, so any particular location experiences it infrequently. The interval varies greatly by location. A wider surrounding region can see a partial solar eclipse.

**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Almost everyone believes the Moon changes shape because Earth's shadow falls on it. Almost everyone is wrong, and by the end of this mission you will be able to prove it with a lamp and a ball.

1. Read **Half Lit, Always** — the whole lesson hangs on one sentence in the second paragraph.
2. Learn the words in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Keep the **One Ball, One Lamp** chart open while you work.
4. Sort the cards in **Phase or Eclipse?** — two of them fool most adults.
5. Take the quiz. Question 3 is the shadow trap.
6. Explain a phase to someone at home using the **Sentence Frames**.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember Half Lit, Always** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Design Challenge: A Moon Model That Cannot Fool Anyone** — build the model, and mark every guess as a guess.

Bonus: look at the real Moon tonight and name its phase before you check. 🌙

Right-lit waxing examples use a northern-up textbook convention; viewing orientation varies with location and time. Dark outlines make the new Moon’s position visible in diagrams, not in the real night sky. All sizes, distances, shadow cones and orbital planes are simplified and not to scale. Lunar surface textures are artistic. Ordinary phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow. Keep the model ball out of the observer’s head shadow for a full phase; deliberately align it only when demonstrating an eclipse. Use a cool lamp and blunt handle with teacher supervision, never direct solar viewing or a laser. Educator review remains pending.
